messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

When Ahmad was 34, he was working late in the quiet basement of the software firm where he had been hired two years earlier. The basement, normally a place of routine keyboard clicks, became a scene of terror when a senior colleague, an older man with a scarred face, pushed him into a corner and forced himself on him. The assault lasted only a few minutes, but Ahmad’s body and mind were left in disarray. The next day, as the company rushed to call emergency services, a blaring siren cut through the office, and ambulances rattled past the building’s windows. Since that night, the sound of sirens has become a constant reminder of that violation, and the sight of an ambulance’s flashing lights triggers the same jolt of fear that once rushed through his chest. He also cannot bear to be alone with other men, especially in places where authority figures are present, because the memory of the attacker’s control clings to him whenever a man’s face looms close. The first weeks after the assault were a blur of panic and avoidance. Whenever he heard sirens or saw an ambulance, Ahmad would bolt for the nearest exit, refusing to stay inside even if the building was safe. He began steering clear of rooms where uniforms or weapons might be displayed, such as the company’s safety training room where police and military officers demonstrated protective gear. When a colleague invited him to a team lunch in a downtown bistro, he declined, saying he was “not feeling up to it.” The more he avoided these environments, the more he began to feel trapped in a narrow circle of “safe” spots—his apartment, the quiet side of the office, and the parking garage on his way home. He began to believe that he was living in a constant state of false alarm, that danger lurked behind every corner. The fear that drove Ahmad’s avoidance also fed his negative appraisals. Every time he found himself in a situation that required him to be around other men or in uniformed settings, he blamed himself for being weak or for not standing up to the assailant. The idea that the assault had happened because of “something I did” gnawed at him. He felt that society had failed to protect him; the justice system had never delivered a conviction, and no one had spoken to him about the injustice that had been inflicted. His sense of loss deepened, and he was certain that he would never again experience “normal” emotions—his happiness, his calm. The more he avoided, the more these self-blame and injustice thoughts hardened, and the more he felt he could not trust any environment to be truly safe. In return, the constant threat of being triggered made his avoidance seem more necessary. Each siren, each ambulance, each moment of male presence felt like a potential repeat of that night, and Ahmad’s mind convinced him that staying away from uniforms and authority figures was the only way to survive. He began to scan his surroundings for danger, looking at every hallway, every security camera, any sign that could signal a threat. That scanning reinforced his sense that he was in danger, even when there was nothing to fear. It also made him even more likely to see threats where none existed, turning mundane office equipment into potential weapons. The cycle tightened. Because Ahmad’s avoidance strategies kept him isolated, he had fewer opportunities to challenge his negative thoughts. When he tried to engage with a coworker over lunch, the conversation was cut short by the loud clatter of a delivery truck’s brakes, and he immediately retreated, fearing the noise might signal an ambulance. The avoidance itself amplified the triggers—every siren he heard or imagined was louder because he had cut off the normal distractions that once balanced his anxiety. Likewise, the threat of danger felt larger because his environment was so narrowly defined that even a simple traffic noise could feel like an impending assault. Months passed, and the software engineer who once coded with confidence now lived in a perpetual state of alert. His work performance suffered; he would pause his coding to stare at the ceiling, convinced a danger was about to manifest. His single status became a shield; he declined invitations to social gatherings where men’s voices would dominate, fearing the slightest threat. When his supervisor asked about a project deadline, Ahmad’s reply was hesitant, a sign of the self-blame that haunted him—he felt that his past had ruined his future. What finally pushed Ahmad to seek help was a break at his job. While working on a critical release, his computer crashed, and he could not recover the data. The loss forced him to confront the reality that his avoidance had cost him professional success. He also began to notice that even his dreams were filled with sirens and ambulance lights, waking him in the night. The cumulative strain on his mental health and his career led him to schedule an appointment with a therapist. He is most afraid that he will never be able to feel normal emotions again, but he also hopes that, through some process, he might learn to trust his surroundings and reclaim the sense of safety that has been stripped from him.
